steps.title: Quality is not preference
steps.body: You may dislike a perfectly made wine, or love a simple one. Quality judgement asks whether the wine is well made and expressive of its style and origin. Preference asks whether you enjoy it. Professionals separate the two: a great Fino can be outstanding even for someone who prefers fruity reds.
steps.highlight: Quality is not the same as liking

steps.title: Criteria and bias
steps.body: Use balance, length, intensity and complexity, plus typicity: does it taste like its grape and place? Bias creeps in through price, label, reputation, glass colour and even music. In blind tests, wine experts have rated the same wine differently when told it was expensive. Tasting blind removes much of this.

steps.prompt: Match each bias to its source.
steps.explanation: Biases are natural; tasting blind and in a fixed order reduce them.

steps.body: Taste the same wine twice in a flight without knowing. If your notes differ a lot, you've just measured your own consistency, a humbling and useful exercise.

steps.prompt: What is the best way to reduce label and price bias?
options: Taste only one wine at a time
steps.explanation: Tasting blind removes the influence of label, price and reputation.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Quality and personal preference are different questions
Judge with balance, length, intensity, complexity and typicity
Blind tasting reduces price and label bias
